title: Study of the First Element - Hydrogen
tagline: Position in the periodic table, preparation from metals, acids, alkalis and water, and the collection and testing of hydrogen gas.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Hydrogen is the simplest element: one proton, one electron, and chemistry built on completing a two-electron shell. This chapter covers its ambiguous position in the periodic table, the laboratory and commercial preparations — with metals and dilute acids, with alkalis, and from water by displacement or electrolysis — and the collection, identification and properties of the gas. Because hydrogen sits with the metals in group 1 yet behaves like the halogens in gaining one electron, it is the classic example that no single rule classifies every element.

learn.title: Position of hydrogen in the periodic table

blocks.text: Hydrogen has atomic number 1 and electronic configuration 1 — a single electron in the K shell. Like the group 1 metals it needs to lose one electron to become H+, and like the halogens it needs to gain one electron to reach the stable duet of two, forming H-. This dual character is why hydrogen is placed with the alkali metals in group 1 (by electron configuration) yet sits apart: unlike them it is a non-metal, it forms only one covalent bond in compounds such as H2O and CH4, and its diatomic molecule H2 is a gas rather than a metal lattice. No single position satisfies every property, and the placement in group 1 with a note of resemblance to halogens is the accepted compromise.

items: Atomic number 1; configuration 1; forms H+ (as in acids) and hydride H- (in metal hydrides).
Like group 1: one outer electron, valency 1, forms compounds like NaCl analogues (NaH).
Unlike group 1: a gas, a non-metal, forms covalent bonds with non-metals.
Like halogens: needs one electron for a full outer shell and is diatomic (H2, like F2, Cl2).
Hydrogen is the lightest substance known — density about one fourteenth that of air.

items.meaning: The K shell is full with two electrons, so hydrogen completes its shell by gaining OR losing one electron.
A compound containing hydrogen as H-, such as sodium hydride NaH.
Existing as molecules of two atoms, as in H2, N2, O2 and the halogens.

blocks.text: In the laboratory, hydrogen is prepared by acting a dilute acid on a metal that lies above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Zinc is the usual choice because it reacts steadily: zinc plus dilute sulphuric acid gives zinc sulphate and hydrogen, and zinc plus dilute hydrochloric acid gives zinc chloride and hydrogen. Metals below hydrogen — copper, silver and gold — do not displace it from acids, which is why copper is used for vessels that must resist acid attack. Hydrogen is also obtained from alkalis: zinc dissolves in sodium hydroxide solution to give sodium zincate and hydrogen, which shows that zinc, like aluminium, has the dual character of a metal and a non-metal.

items.note: Use DILUTE acid; concentrated sulphuric acid gives sulphur dioxide instead of hydrogen.
Two HCl molecules are needed to balance two chlorides in ZnCl2.
Hydrogen from alkali proves zinc's amphoteric nature — it reacts with both acids and bases.
Copper lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid.

items: Choose a metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb.
Use dilute acids — the acid must be dilute so that hydrogen and not a reduction product of the concentrated acid is evolved.
Granulated zinc is used because its rough surface speeds the reaction; dropwise acid addition controls it.
Alkali route: Zn or Al + NaOH solution gives the zincate/aluminate salt and hydrogen.
The apparatus must be airtight — a trace of air with hydrogen forms an explosive mixture.

items.meaning: A metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series replacing it from an acid.
Na2ZnO2, the salt formed when zinc dissolves in sodium hydroxide solution.
Order of metals by readiness to lose electrons; hydrogen is the reference element in it.

blocks.text: Water is the chief source of hydrogen on an industrial scale. Passing steam over red-hot iron gives iron(II,III) oxide and hydrogen — the historical and still-demonstrated reaction 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. Electrolysis of water, made conducting by a little dilute sulphuric acid, splits it into hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode in a 2:1 volume ratio — the classic hydrogen-oxygen ratio experiment. Sodium and potassium react with cold water to give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen, while magnesium reacts only with hot water and iron reacts with steam; this graded reactivity is exactly the pattern the reactivity series describes.

items.note: Hydrogen is collected over water; the reaction stops when heating stops.
Volume ratio 2:1 hydrogen to oxygen; hydrogen collects at the cathode (negative electrode).
Violent at room temperature; the alkali formed makes the solution turn red litmus blue.

items.text: Magnesium with steam: Mg + H2O ->(hot) MgO + H2. With hot water magnesium reacts slowly to give magnesium hydroxide: Mg + 2H2O -> Mg(OH)2 + H2.
items.note: Cold water barely attacks magnesium — heat is needed, unlike sodium; the oxide forms with steam, the hydroxide with liquid hot water.

items: Increasing reactivity with water: K and Na react violently even with cold water; Ca and Mg slowly with cold; Mg, Fe, Zn with steam.
Electrolysis needs an electrolyte — dilute sulphuric acid or sodium hydroxide — because pure water conducts very poorly.
Equal volumes of water produces 2:1 hydrogen:oxygen by volume, matching the formula H2O.
Hydrogen from water displacement is collected over water because it is insoluble.

blocks.text: Hydrogen is insoluble in water, so it is collected over water — a jar inverted in the trough, with the water displaced downward as gas enters. Because it is much lighter than air it may also be collected in an inverted jar by the downward displacement of air: the rising hydrogen pushes the heavier air down and out. Identification is by the pop test: a lighted splint at the jar's mouth gives a sharp squeaky pop, which is the sound of hydrogen burning explosively with the oxygen in the air. Pure hydrogen burns quietly with a pale blue flame. In its reactions hydrogen acts both as a reducer (removing oxygen from copper oxide) and as a fuel (releasing heat as it burns).

items.text: Test: bring a lighted splint to the jar — a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen.
items.note: A weak, brief pop can indicate a mixture of hydrogen and air; a loud sharp pop indicates reasonably pure hydrogen.

items.text: Reduction: H2 + CuO ->(heat) Cu + H2O. Black copper oxide turns red-brown as copper forms.
items.note: Hydrogen removes oxygen — it is the reducing agent, and water droplets condense on the cooler tube.

items.text: Combustion: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O with a pale blue flame.
items.note: The only product is water — hydrogen burning is a pollution-free reaction.

items: Colourless, odourless, tasteless — the squeaky pop is the only practical identification.
Insoluble in water; density about 0.09 g per litre against air at 1.29 g per litre.
Collects over water (insoluble) or by downward displacement of air (lighter than air).
Burns in air with a pale blue flame; the mixture with air (or oxygen) is explosive, so tests are never run on a closed jar.
Acts as a reducing agent on metal oxides, and the water formed turns anhydrous copper sulphate blue.

items.meaning: Collecting a gas lighter than air in an inverted jar; the gas rises and the air is pushed down.
The sharp sound made by burning hydrogen brought into contact with a lighted splint — the confirmatory test.
A substance that removes oxygen from another substance; hydrogen reduces copper oxide to copper.

figures.caption: Figure: Laboratory preparation of hydrogen
figures.description: Wool bed supports granulated zinc in a flask; dilute sulphuric acid added from a dropping funnel reacts steadily; hydrogen passes through the delivery tube and is collected over water in an inverted jar until no more water remains displaced.

figures.caption: Figure: Reactivity series position of hydrogen
figures.description: Metals above hydrogen (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb) displace it from dilute acids; metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au) do not — hydrogen is the dividing reference element.

keyPoints: Hydrogen: Z = 1, configuration 1, placed in group 1 but resembling halogens by needing one electron.
Lab preparation: metal above hydrogen + dilute acid -> salt + hydrogen; zinc is the standard metal.
Copper and metals below hydrogen do not displace hydrogen from acids.
Zinc with sodium hydroxide gives sodium zincite and hydrogen — zinc is amphoteric.
From water: steam over hot iron gives Fe3O4 and H2; electrolysis gives H2 and O2 in 2:1 volume ratio.
Reactivity with water: K/Na violent with cold; Mg/Fe need heat or steam.
Hydrogen is insoluble in water (collect over water) and lighter than air (downward displacement of air).
Confirmatory test: sharp squeaky pop with a lighted splint.
Hydrogen reduces copper oxide to copper and burns with a pale blue flame to give only water.
examFocus: Preparation questions need equation, conditions and collection method — name the acid as dilute, because concentrated acid changes the product.
The reactivity-series reasoning (above/below hydrogen) earns the mark for 'why this metal' questions.
State volumes, not just gases: electrolysis of water is asked as a 2:1 hydrogen:oxygen volume ratio.
Safety points count: never test hydrogen in a closed jar; test it at the mouth of the jar.

vocabulary.meaning: Stable two-electron arrangement of the K shell.
Salt formed by zinc with sodium hydroxide, Na2ZnO2.
Squeaky sound identifying hydrogen with a lighted splint.
Removes oxygen from another substance; hydrogen is one.
A more reactive metal replacing hydrogen from an acid.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen is placed in group 1 of the periodic table because:
options: It is a metal like lithium
Its atom has one outer electron
It has the highest atomic mass
questions.answer: Its atom has one outer electron
questions.explanation: Group 1 membership follows from the single electron in the outer shell, just like sodium; hydrogen's non-metallic properties make the placement a compromise.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 'it is a metal' — hydrogen is a non-metal placed by configuration, not by character.

questions.prompt: Which metal will NOT liberate hydrogen from dilute sulphuric acid?
questions.explanation: Copper lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid; zinc, iron and magnesium all lie above it.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming every metal reacts with acid — the position relative to hydrogen decides.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen is collected by downward displacement of air because it is:
options: Denser than air and soluble in water
Lighter than air and insoluble in water
Soluble in water and reactive with air
questions.answer: Lighter than air and insoluble in water
questions.explanation: Its low density lets it rise and push air downward out of the inverted jar, and insolubility also allows collection over water.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one reason — the method is justified by density, and the water method by insolubility.

questions.prompt: The confirmatory test for hydrogen is a:
options: Squeaky pop with a lighted splint
questions.answer: Squeaky pop with a lighted splint
questions.explanation: Hydrogen burns explosively with air at the splint, producing the characteristic squeaky pop.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing it with the carbon dioxide test, which uses lime water turning milky.

questions.prompt: When steam is passed over red-hot iron, the products are:
questions.explanation: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2; the mixed-valence oxide Fe3O4 is magnetite and hydrogen is the gas evolved.
questions.commonMistake: Writing Fe2O3 — the steam-iron reaction gives Fe3O4, not rust.

questions.prompt: Electrolysis of acidified water produces hydrogen and oxygen in a volume ratio of:
questions.explanation: 2H2O gives 2H2 + O2, so twice the volume of hydrogen is produced compared with oxygen — the ratio that matches the formula H2O.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the ratio by reading the equation right to left.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give ________ salt and ________ gas.
questions.explanation: Zn + H2SO4(dilute) -> ZnSO4 + H2; the metal above hydrogen displaces it from the acid.
questions.commonMistake: Naming zinc chloride — that product comes from hydrochloric acid, not sulphuric acid.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when zinc is treated with sodium hydroxide solution, the salt formed is ________ and hydrogen is evolved.
questions.explanation: Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2; the reaction shows zinc's dual (amphoteric) character.
questions.commonMistake: Writing zinc hydroxide — the hydroxide is an intermediate that dissolves in excess alkali to give the zincate.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for the laboratory preparation of hydrogen using hydrochloric acid, and state why the acid must be dilute.
questions.answer: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. The acid must be dilute because concentrated acids are oxidising: with concentrated sulphuric acid, for example, sulphur dioxide is evolved instead of hydrogen (Zn + 2H2SO4(conc.) -> ZnSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O), so no hydrogen is obtained.
questions.explanation: Dilute acid provides H+ ions that the metal displaces as H2; the concentrated acid reacts as an oxidising agent and gives oxide gases instead.
questions.commonMistake: Saying 'it would be too fast' — the reason is the change of products, not the reaction rate.

questions.prompt: Explain why hydrogen resembles both group 1 elements and the halogens.
questions.answer: Like the group 1 elements, hydrogen has one outer electron (configuration 1), shows valency 1 and can lose that electron to form H+, as in acidic solutions. Like the halogens, it needs one electron to complete its outer shell (the duet of two), so it can gain an electron to form H-, and it exists as diatomic molecules such as H2. Unlike group 1 it is a non-metal and forms covalent bonds, which is why no single group position satisfies all its properties.
questions.explanation: The comparison is drawn from electronic configuration in both directions: losing one electron (metals) and gaining one (halogens).
questions.commonMistake: Describing only one side of the resemblance; full marks need both the group 1 and the halogen parallel.

questions.prompt: Describe two laboratory methods of preparing hydrogen other than with an acid, with equations, and state how the gas is collected in each case.
questions.answer: (1) From alkalis: zinc (or aluminium) dissolves in sodium hydroxide solution: Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2. (2) From water: steam passed over red-hot iron gives 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2, and electrolysis of acidified water gives 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2. Hydrogen is collected over water in all cases because it is insoluble in water.
questions.explanation: All three routes give hydrogen without an acid; collection over water is universal here because of insolubility.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that the alkali method needs an amphoteric metal — reacting sodium with sodium hydroxide makes no sense.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen reduces heated copper oxide. Write the equation, name what happens to hydrogen and to copper oxide, describe the observations, and identify the test for the product formed.
questions.answer: H2 + CuO ->(heat) Cu + H2O. Hydrogen removes oxygen from copper oxide, so hydrogen is the reducing agent and copper oxide is reduced to copper. Observations: the black copper oxide powder turns red-brown as metallic copper forms, and droplets of a colourless liquid (water) condense on the cooler parts of the tube. The product is confirmed by the test for water: white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate turns blue when the liquid is added.
questions.explanation: Reduction is loss of oxygen by the oxide; the observations follow from copper metal forming and water condensing, and the water is identified with anhydrous CuSO4.
questions.commonMistake: Saying hydrogen is 'oxidised to water' without naming it the reducing agent — both roles (agent and product) are usually required.

questions.prompt: Why is granulated zinc preferred to zinc dust, and why must the apparatus for generating hydrogen be kept airtight?
questions.answer: Granulated zinc has a rough, porous surface with a large effective area, giving a steady, controllable rate of reaction; fine zinc dust reacts too vigorously and can be carried into the delivery tube, and it may also contain soluble impurities. The apparatus must be airtight because a mixture of hydrogen with air (or oxygen) is explosive: any leak lets air in, and a flame near a leaking apparatus could ignite the mixture inside. An airtight train also prevents the collected gas from being diluted, so the pop test gives a reliable result.
questions.explanation: One reason concerns rate and purity of generation; the other concerns the explosive limits of hydrogen-air mixtures and the reliability of collection.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only the 'too fast' part of the first half and missing that hydrogen-air mixtures are explosive.
